x: The diurnal range is highest in north-western India during winter, where it is about 14°–18°C.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Temperature generally decreases from the equator towards the poles.
The sea moderates temperature, making coastal climates more equable.
Interior areas generally have a smaller annual temperature range than coastal areas.
Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude.
x: Option C is incorrect: interior areas have a larger annual range, because land heats and cools fast. Coasts are equable because the sea moderates them.

s: Where is the annual range of temperature largest?
o: High-latitude continental interiors such as Siberia
x: The annual range is largest in high-latitude continental interiors like Siberia and minimum at the equator; coasts have a small range.

s: Where in Andhra Pradesh is a high diurnal range of temperature found?
x: The coast has a low diurnal range moderated by the sea and sea breezes (as at Visakhapatnam and Kakinada), while interior Rayalaseema has a high range.

s: Where is the annual range of temperature minimum?
x: The annual range is smallest at the Equator and largest in high-latitude continental interiors such as Siberia.

s: Where is the seasonal range of temperature maximum?
x: Seasonal range is maximum in high latitudes (APPSC-G1 2023) and minimum at the Equator.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about insolation?
o: The angle of the Sun's rays affects the insolation received at a place.
The length of the day affects the insolation received at a place.
Atmospheric transparency has no effect on the insolation received.
The slope and aspect of the land affect the insolation received.
x: Atmospheric transparency does influence insolation, along with the angle of the rays, duration of sunshine, and slope and aspect of land.

s: Which one of the following correctly represents the Earth's aphelion?
x: Aphelion occurs around 4 July, when the Earth is approximately 152 million kilometres from the Sun.

s: Why do the highest temperatures on Earth generally occur in the sub-tropical deserts rather than at the Equator?
o: The maximum annual rainfall of the deserts
The permanent presence of cold ocean currents
Persistent cloud cover and humid air
x: Sub-tropical deserts around 20°–30° N have clear skies and dry air, permitting very high temperatures; the Equator does not record the highest temperatures merely because it receives strong insolation.

s: At the same latitude, insolation is generally higher over:
o: Polar seas than over tropical land
x: Insolation declines towards the poles and, at the same latitude, is higher over continents than over oceans.

s: In the Earth's heat budget, where is a heat surplus found?
x: The tropics have a heat surplus and the poles a deficit; winds and ocean currents carry heat poleward.

s: What type of the Sun's rays does the equator receive, causing it to be heated more than the poles?
x: Latitude sets the Sun's angle: the equator gets more direct rays and greater heating, while the poles get oblique rays and lower heating.

s: On about which date is the Earth at perihelion, its closest point to the Sun?
x: Perihelion falls around 3 January (about 147 million km); aphelion around 4 July.

s: What is the approximate Earth–Sun distance at perihelion?
x: The Earth is about 147 million km from the Sun at perihelion and about 152 million km at aphelion.

s: How does insolation received at the Earth's surface generally change from the Equator towards the poles?
x: The Equator gets direct rays and the poles oblique rays, so insolation falls poleward.

s: Which of the following describes a heat dome?
o: A cold ocean current remains below a stationary cyclone
A low-pressure system forms over a rapidly moving jet stream
A monsoon trough shifts permanently towards the poles
A stalled high-pressure system remains under a slowed, meandering jet stream
x: A heat dome develops when a high-pressure system stalls beneath a slowed and meandering jet stream, producing persistent heat.

s: Why is an urban heat island primarily produced?
o: cities receive no long-wave radiation at night.
rural vegetation reflects all incoming radiation toward cities.
urban areas are always located at lower latitudes than rural areas.
concrete and asphalt store heat and make cities warmer than surrounding rural areas.
x: Concrete and asphalt absorb and retain heat, causing urban areas to be warmer than their rural surroundings.

s: Under IMD heatwave criteria, what is the minimum threshold temperature for coastal areas?
x: A heatwave needs at least 37°C on the coast, 40°C in the plains and 30°C in the hills.

s: Under IMD criteria, what is the minimum-temperature threshold for a cold wave in hilly regions?
x: The hilly-region cold-wave threshold is 0°C or below; 10°C or below is the threshold for the plains.

s: TRISHNA, a thermal-infrared satellite mission, is a joint venture of ISRO and which agency?
x: TRISHNA is an Indo-French ISRO-CNES mission to map energy and water budgets, land surface temperature and urban heat islands; its PSLV launch is due in 2027.

s: Which is identified as the hottest place in Andhra Pradesh?
x: Rentachintala in Palnadu is the hottest place in Andhra Pradesh, while Lambasingi is the coolest.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Dras in Ladakh recorded approximately −45°C in 1908. Death Valley is associated with 56.7°C, while Vostok is associated with −89.2°C.

s: Since which year has Andhra Pradesh had a Heat Wave Action Plan?
x: Andhra Pradesh has had a Heat Wave Action Plan since 2016; APSDMA also sends district-wise SMS heat-wave alerts.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about heatwave criteria?
o: In the plains, a severe heatwave is declared at an actual maximum temperature of 45°C or more.
In the plains, a heatwave is a departure from normal of 4.5°C to 6.4°C.
In the plains, a severe heatwave is a departure from normal of more than 6.4°C.
In coastal areas, a departure of 4.5°C or more counts as a heatwave when the maximum is at least 37°C.
x: A severe heatwave by actual maximum temperature in the plains needs 47°C or more, not 45°C.

s: In the plains, at what actual maximum temperature is a severe heatwave declared?
x: In the plains an actual maximum of 45°C or more counts as a heatwave and 47°C or more as a severe heatwave.

s: Where was the world's coldest recorded temperature of −89.2°C recorded?
x: Vostok holds the world record of −89.2°C; Dras is India's coldest and Death Valley the world's hottest.

s: Which place is called the 'Kashmir of Andhra Pradesh'?
x: Lambasingi in ASR district, about 2°C, is the coldest place in AP; Rentachintala is the hottest.

s: What departure from the normal maximum temperature marks a severe heatwave?
x: A departure of 4.5–6.4°C is a heatwave; above 6.4°C is a severe heatwave.

s: Where was Andhra Pradesh's 2026 peak temperature of 48.1°C recorded?
x: The 2026 peak of 48.1°C was recorded at Piduguralla in Palnadu on 21 May 2026.

s: In which year did NDMA issue its heat-wave guidelines?
x: NDMA first issued its heat-wave guidelines ('Guidelines for Preparation of Action Plan – Prevention and Management of Heat-Wave') in 2016; 2017 and 2019 are revised editions. AP's Heat Wave Action Plan also dates from 2016.

s: According to the India Meteorological Department, what is the minimum maximum-temperature threshold for a heat wave in the plains?
x: IMD considers a heat wave in the plains only when the maximum is at least 40°C (37°C on the coast, 30°C in the hills).

s: Which of the following districts was listed as a severe-heatwave district in Andhra Pradesh's Heat Action Plan 2026?
x: Palnadu, with Tirupati, Prakasam, SPSR Nellore, Markapuram, Guntur and Bapatla, was a severe-heatwave district in HAP 2026.

s:
Consider the following statements about IMD criteria:
1. A heat wave in coastal areas needs a maximum temperature of at least 37°C.
2. A cold wave in the plains needs a minimum temperature of 10°C or below.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: IMD uses 37°C as the coastal heat-wave threshold and 10°C or below as the cold-wave minimum for the plains.

s: Where was the world's highest temperature of 56.7°C recorded?
x: Death Valley holds the world record of 56.7°C; Vostok holds the coldest (-89.2°C).

s: Why does temperature normally decrease with increasing altitude?
o: Higher air receives more long-wave radiation from the Sun.
The ground heats the air from below, while higher air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust.
The Earth stops emitting radiation above the lower atmosphere.
The atmosphere is heated mainly from above by direct solar radiation.
x: The ground heats the atmosphere from below. At higher levels the air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust, so it absorbs less heat.

s: Which climatic control explains why the Himalayas are cooler despite their lower latitude?
x: Altitude makes the Himalayas cool despite their low latitude, since temperature falls about 6.5°C per km.

s: What is the normal lapse rate, at which temperature falls with increasing height in the troposphere?
x: Temperature normally falls with height at about 6.5 °C per km, because the air is heated from below and higher air absorbs less heat.

s: Which of the following is NOT a reason why temperature falls with height in the troposphere?
o: The air is heated from below by the ground.
Higher air holds less water vapour and dust.
Higher air is heated directly by the Sun more than lower air.
x: Air is heated from below, not directly by the Sun; thinner air with less vapour and dust aloft makes temperature fall with height.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about factors affecting temperature?
o: Cold ocean currents raise coastal temperatures.
Continentality produces extreme interior climates with a large annual range.
Cloud cover reduces daytime heating and night-time cooling.
Warm ocean currents raise coastal temperatures.
x: Cold ocean currents lower coastal temperatures and favour west-coast deserts; it is warm currents that raise them.

s: How do isotherms in the Northern Hemisphere bend in January?
o: Equatorward over both land and oceans
Poleward over land and equatorward over oceans
Equatorward over land and poleward over oceans
x: In January, Northern Hemisphere isotherms bend equatorward over colder landmasses and poleward over relatively warmer oceans.

s: In winter, India's 20°C isotherm runs approximately from the mouth of the Tapi to which delta?
x: In winter the 20°C isotherm runs from the Tapi mouth to the Mahanadi delta; temperature rises from north to south.

s: Which of the following defines the thermal equator?
o: line joining places of highest mean temperature, generally lying north of the geographical Equator.
boundary between the tropical and polar zones, fixed at 23½° latitude.
line joining the coldest places in both hemispheres.
geographical Equator, which never shifts seasonally.
x: The thermal equator is the line of highest mean temperature. It lies mostly north of the geographical Equator and shifts with the apparent movement of the Sun.

s: What are lines joining places having equal temperature called?
x: Isotherms join places of equal temperature; they generally run east-west and are more regular in the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere.

s: How do isotherms in the Northern Hemisphere bend in July?
o: Equatorward over land and poleward over oceans
Poleward over both land and oceans
Equatorward over both land and oceans
Poleward over land and equatorward over oceans
x: In July isotherms bend poleward over land and the reverse over oceans; January shows the opposite pattern.

s: Why are isotherms more regular in the Southern Hemisphere?
o: Closer to the Sun in July
x: The Southern Hemisphere is mostly ocean, so its isotherms run more regularly east-west.

s: What does the Northern Hemisphere have that makes the thermal equator lie mostly north of the Equator?
x: The thermal equator, the line of highest mean temperature, lies mostly north of the Equator because there is more land there.

s: Which January isotherm divides India into tropical and sub-tropical parts?
x: The January 18°C isotherm separates tropical south India from sub-tropical north India.

s: In a valley inversion, why is the valley floor colder than the slopes?
o: warm air flows downslope and accumulates at the valley floor.
the valley floor is always nearer to the Sun.
cold air drains downslope and settles in the valley.
the slopes receive no solar radiation in winter.
x: Cold, dense air flows downslope and accumulates in valleys, producing frost pockets while the slopes remain relatively warmer.

s: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Frontal inversion — association with a frontal boundary
Valley inversion — downslope drainage of cold air
Surface or radiation inversion — night-time cooling of the ground
Stratosphere — absence of any inversion condition
x: The stratosphere is a permanent inversion layer, so it is incorrect to associate it with the absence of inversion.

s: What is a condition in which temperature rises with height instead of falling called?
x: In a temperature inversion the normal lapse rate reverses; it is favoured by long winter nights, clear skies and calm dry air.

s: Fog, frost, smog and the trapping of pollutants in the planetary boundary layer are effects of which condition?
x: Temperature inversions can produce fog, frost and smog and trap pollutants within the planetary boundary layer.

s: Which layer of the atmosphere is a permanent inversion layer?
x: The stratosphere is the permanent inversion layer, where temperature rises with height.

s: Which of the following does NOT favour a temperature inversion?
x: Inversions need long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air and snow cover; cloudy skies do not favour them.

s: In valleys with temperature inversion, why are orchards usually planted on upper slopes?
o: Frost pockets form on the valley floor
Valley floors are warmer at night
Upper slopes are colder at night
x: Cold air drains into the valley floor and forms frost pockets, while the slopes stay warmer.
